_note: Hand-checked 'Did you know' facts for Benflix title pages, Home and the screensaver. Key: "Name (Year)" as Jellyfin shows it, or an IMDb number like "tt4589218". Each fact must be a fun, surprising, true story (behind the scenes, trivia, Easter eggs), NOT plain information like who directed it, what it's based on, where it was filmed, release dates, budgets or awards. Keep each under about 170 characters, family-friendly and spoiler-free. Tower downloads this file every night.
Five Nights at Freddy's (2023): The animatronics in Five Nights at Freddy's are real, not computer-made. They were built by Jim Henson's Creature Shop.
Foxy was the hardest animatronic to work, needing a team of puppeteers to bring him to life.
Getting performers into the heavy animatronic suits first took about an hour. The crew got it down to a few minutes.
Scott Cawthon, who made the original Five Nights at Freddy's games, co-wrote the movie's script.
YouTuber MatPat, famous for his Game Theory videos about the games, has a cameo as a diner waiter.
YouTuber CoryxKenshin, who played the games on his channel, makes a cameo as a taxi driver.
Five Nights at Freddy's came out in theaters and on Peacock on the same day, and still became Blumhouse's biggest opening ever.
13 Hours: The Secret Soldiers of Benghaz: Members of the real security team worked with the 13 Hours crew to get the details right.
21 (2008): Jeff Ma, the real MIT student the movie's hero is based on, has a cameo as a blackjack dealer.
50/50 (2011): 50/50 is based on writer Will Reiser's own fight with cancer in his twenties.
Seth Rogen really was Will Reiser's friend while he was sick, and the movie's best friend is based on him.
Joseph Gordon-Levitt really shaved his head on camera for 50/50, so they only had one take.
A Beautiful Day in the Neighborhood (201: Tom Hanks found out he is a distant cousin of Fred Rogers, the man he plays.
A Beautiful Day in the Neighborhood was filmed in Pittsburgh, including the real studio where Mister Rogers' Neighborhood was made.
About Time (2013): Richard Curtis, who wrote Love Actually and Notting Hill, said About Time would be the last movie he directed.
13 Going on 30 (2004): Brie Larson, years before Captain Marvel, has a small role in 13 Going on 30 as one of the popular girls.
9 (2009): 9 grew out of Shane Acker's short film of the same name, which was nominated for an Oscar.
Adrift (2018): Adrift was filmed out on the open ocean near Fiji, and Shailene Woodley did a lot of her own sailing.
A Bronx Tale (1993): A Bronx Tale began as Chazz Palminteri's one-man stage show about his own childhood in the Bronx.
A Christmas Carol (1951): In Britain, the 1951 A Christmas Carol came out under the name Scrooge.
After Earth (2013): The story idea for After Earth came from Will Smith, who stars next to his real son Jaden.
Airheads (1994): The rock band White Zombie makes a cameo in Airheads.
American Hustle (2013): Christian Bale gained about 40 pounds and hurt his back playing Irving Rosenfeld.
David O. Russell let the cast make up a lot of American Hustle's dialogue as they went.
American Movie: The Making of Northweste: American Movie follows a real Wisconsin filmmaker, Mark Borchardt, trying to finish a tiny horror movie. It won the top documentary prize at Sundance.
American Underdog (2021): Before he became an NFL star, the real Kurt Warner stocked shelves at a grocery store, just like in American Underdog.
Angels in the Outfield (1994): A young Joseph Gordon-Levitt stars in Angels in the Outfield, and Matthew McConaughey and Adrien Brody have small roles.
Anger Management (2003): Anger Management is full of cameos, including tennis star John McEnroe and basketball coach Bobby Knight.
Aniara (2018): Aniara is based on a 1956 Swedish poem by Harry Martinson, who later won the Nobel Prize in Literature.
Annihilation (2018): Alex Garland wrote Annihilation from his memory of Jeff VanderMeer's novel, without rereading the book.
Around the World in 80 Days (2004): Jackie Chan plays Passepartout in this Around the World in 80 Days, and did his own stunts.
Arnold Schwarzenegger has a cameo as Prince Hapi.
Austin Powers: The Spy Who Shagged Me (1: Mike Myers plays three parts in this Austin Powers: Austin, Dr. Evil and Fat Bastard.
Mini-Me is played by Verne Troyer, who was 2 feet 8 inches tall.
Bad Teacher (2011): Cameron Diaz and Justin Timberlake had dated for years before they played love interests in Bad Teacher.
Barbarian (2022): Barbarian's writer and director, Zach Cregger, started out in the comedy group The Whitest Kids U' Know.
BASEketball (1998): BASEketball stars Trey Parker and Matt Stone, the creators of South Park, and was directed by Airplane!'s David Zucker.
BASEketball is a real game. Director David Zucker and his friends made it up in his driveway years before the movie.
Beavis and Butt-Head Do the Universe (20: Mike Judge voices both Beavis and Butt-Head, just as he did in the 1990s.
Bee Movie (2007): Jerry Seinfeld came up with Bee Movie from a silly pun he made over dinner with Steven Spielberg.
Beethoven (1992): John Hughes co-wrote Beethoven under a made-up name, Edmond Dantès, the hero of The Count of Monte Cristo.
Big Daddy (1999): Twins Cole and Dylan Sprouse shared the role of Julian in Big Daddy, years before The Suite Life of Zack and Cody.
Big Fat Liar (2002): Much of Big Fat Liar was filmed on the real Universal Studios lot in Hollywood.
Birds of Prey (and the Fantabulous Emanc: Margot Robbie pitched the idea of a Harley Quinn girl-gang movie to Warner Bros. herself, and produced it.
Blazing Saddles (1974): Richard Pryor was one of the writers of Blazing Saddles.
Mel Brooks plays two parts in Blazing Saddles, including the silly Governor Le Petomane.
The campfire beans scene in Blazing Saddles is often called the first fart joke in a big Hollywood movie.
Bo Burnham: Inside (2021): Bo Burnham made Inside completely alone in one room of his guest house, over about a year.
Brightburn (2019): Brightburn was produced by James Gunn and written by his brother Brian and cousin Mark.
Casper (1995): Casper was one of the first movies to have a main character made completely by computer.
Cats & Dogs (2001): Cats & Dogs mixed real trained animals with puppets and computer effects.
Cave of Forgotten Dreams (2010): Werner Herzog filmed Cave of Forgotten Dreams in 3D inside France's Chauvet Cave, where only a tiny crew was allowed in for short visits.
Chappie (2015): Sharlto Copley played Chappie on set, and his performance was turned into the robot with computer effects.
Ninja and Yolandi, who play themselves in Chappie, are the South African rap group Die Antwoord.
Christopher Robin (2018): Jim Cummings voices both Winnie the Pooh and Tigger in Christopher Robin.
City of Ember (2008): City of Ember's underground city was built inside the old Paint Hall at Belfast's shipyard, which later held sets for Game of Thrones.
Class Action Park (2020): Class Action Park is about the real Action Park in New Jersey, a water park famous for its wild rides.
Clockstoppers (2002): Clockstoppers was directed by Jonathan Frakes, who played Commander Riker on Star Trek: The Next Generation.
Cold Pursuit (2019): Cold Pursuit is a remake of the Norwegian movie In Order of Disappearance, by the same director, Hans Petter Moland.
Coneheads (1993): Coneheads grew out of a Saturday Night Live sketch, and Dan Aykroyd and Jane Curtin played the same parts again.
Chris Rock: Tamborine (2018): Chris Rock: Tamborine was directed by Bo Burnham.
Chris Rock: Kill the Messenger (2008): Kill the Messenger was filmed in three cities, Johannesburg, London and New York, and edited together into one show.
Chris Rock: Selective Outrage (2023): Selective Outrage was the first comedy special Netflix ever streamed live.
All the Way (2016): Bryan Cranston plays President Lyndon B. Johnson in All the Way. He won a Tony Award for the same part on Broadway.
Always Be My Maybe (2019): Keanu Reeves plays a funny version of himself in Always Be My Maybe.
Allegiant (2016): Allegiant was meant to be followed by one more Divergent movie, but it was never made.
Constantine (2005): Tilda Swinton plays the angel Gabriel in Constantine.
Contagion (2011): The Contagion team worked with real disease experts, including scientists from the CDC, to make the outbreak believable.
Corpse Bride (2005): Corpse Bride was made with stop-motion puppets, moved by hand a tiny bit for every frame.
Crazy, Stupid, Love. (2011): Crazy, Stupid, Love. was the first of three movies Ryan Gosling and Emma Stone made together, before Gangster Squad and La La Land.
Cruella (2021): Cruella's costumes, more than 270 of them, were made by Jenny Beavan, who won an Oscar for them.
D.A.R.Y.L. (1985): D.A.R.Y.L. stands for Data Analyzing Robot Youth Lifeform.
Dark Shadows (2012): Dark Shadows is based on a 1960s daytime TV soap opera. Its original star, Jonathan Frid, has a cameo.
Darkest Hour (2017): Gary Oldman spent about 200 hours in the makeup chair to become Winston Churchill, and won the Oscar for Best Actor.
Makeup artist Kazu Hiro came out of retirement to do Gary Oldman's Churchill makeup.
Dawn of the Planet of the Apes (2014): Andy Serkis played Caesar on location with motion-capture dots, so the apes were filmed in the real forest instead of a studio.
Death at a Funeral (2010): Death at a Funeral (2010) is a remake of a British movie from just three years earlier. Peter Dinklage plays the same part in both.
Death at a Funeral (2007): Death at a Funeral was directed by Frank Oz, the voice of Yoda and Miss Piggy.
Deepwater Horizon (2016): The Deepwater Horizon crew built an almost full-size copy of the oil rig in a giant tank in Louisiana.
Despicable Me (2010): The Minions' language mixes words from Spanish, French, Italian, English and even food names.
The Minions are voiced by the directors, Pierre Coffin and Chris Renaud.
Divergent (2014): Divergent is based on Veronica Roth's novel, which she wrote while still in college.
DodgeBall: A True Underdog Story (2004): Ben Stiller wore fake teeth and a fake mustache to play White Goodman in DodgeBall.
Real dodgeball coaches trained the DodgeBall cast for weeks.
Don't Look Up (2021): Some of Jonah Hill's lines in Don't Look Up were made up on the spot during filming.
Downsizing (2017): The tiny people in Downsizing were made by filming the actors on oversized sets and props.
Drumline (2002): The Drumline cast went to a drumming boot camp and learned to play for real.
Dungeons & Dragons: Honor Among Thieves: Many of the creatures in Honor Among Thieves were real puppets and costumes on set, not only computer effects.
Eurovision Song Contest: The Story of Fi: Will Ferrell has been a fan of Eurovision since his wife's family in Sweden got him to watch it.
The real town of Húsavík in Iceland made its own campaign video to help the movie's song Husavik win an Oscar.
Evil Dead (2013): Evil Dead (2013) used almost no computer effects. Most of the blood and gore was real makeup and props.
Eye in the Sky (2015): Eye in the Sky was Alan Rickman's last on-screen role.
Finch (2021): Caleb Landry Jones played the robot Jeff on set in a motion-capture suit, often walking on stilts.
Fury (2014): Fury used a real Tiger tank from the Tank Museum in England, the first time a working Tiger appeared in a movie since World War II.
The Fury cast went through a tough army-style boot camp before filming.
Gemini Man (2019): The young Will Smith in Gemini Man was made completely by computer, using Will Smith's own performance.
Get Him to the Greek (2010): Russell Brand's Aldous Snow first appeared in Forgetting Sarah Marshall before getting his own movie.
Gone in Sixty Seconds (2000): The star car, a 1967 Shelby Mustang named Eleanor, became famous on its own.
Green Book (2018): Green Book won the Oscar for Best Picture. The Green Book was a real travel guide for Black drivers in the 1930s to 60s.
Greyhound (2020): Tom Hanks wrote the Greyhound screenplay himself, based on C.S. Forester's novel The Good Shepherd.
Parts of Greyhound were filmed on the USS Kidd, a real World War II destroyer that's now a museum.
Hanna (2011): The Chemical Brothers made the Hanna soundtrack.
Hardcore Henry (2015): Hardcore Henry was filmed almost entirely through GoPro cameras on a stunt person's head, so you see everything through Henry's eyes.
Harry and the Hendersons (1987): Rick Baker's Bigfoot suit for Harry and the Hendersons won the Oscar for Best Makeup.
Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows: Pa: Deathly Hallows: Part 2 was the last of the eight Harry Potter movies, made over about ten years with the same main cast.
Hit Man (2023): Hit Man is loosely based on the real Gary Johnson, a Houston teacher who posed as a hitman for the police.
Hocus Pocus 2 (2022): Hocus Pocus 2 came out 29 years after the first movie, with Bette Midler, Sarah Jessica Parker and Kathy Najimy back as the sisters.
Horrible Bosses (2011): Jennifer Aniston, Kevin Spacey and Colin Farrell play the three bosses. Colin Farrell came up with his character's comb-over look himself.
Hubie Halloween (2020): Hubie Halloween was filmed in Massachusetts, around the real town of Salem.
Hustle (2022): Many real NBA players appear in Hustle, and the hero's discovery, Juancho Hernangómez, is a real NBA player.
I Am Mother (2019): The robot Mother was a real suit made by Weta Workshop, worn by actor Luke Hawker, and voiced by Rose Byrne.
The 7th Voyage of Sinbad (1958): The creatures in The 7th Voyage of Sinbad were brought to life by stop-motion legend Ray Harryhausen.
The Adam Project (2022): The Adam Project's script was around for years. Tom Cruise was once going to star in it.
The Ballad of Buster Scruggs (2018): The Ballad of Buster Scruggs started out as a planned TV series by the Coen brothers.
The Bank Job (2008): The Bank Job is based on a real 1971 London bank robbery, the Baker Street robbery.
The Batman (2022): The Batmobile in The Batman was a real working car built for the movie.
Much of The Batman's Gotham was made with giant LED screens behind the actors, like on The Mandalorian.
The Big Short (2015): Adam McKay had celebrities like Margot Robbie break the fourth wall to explain tricky money ideas.
The Boondock Saints (1999): Writer-director Troy Duffy wrote The Boondock Saints while working as a bartender in Los Angeles.
The Bucket List (2007): The Bucket List made the phrase bucket list popular around the world.
The Butler (2013): The Butler is inspired by Eugene Allen, who worked as a butler at the White House for 34 years.
The Cabin in the Woods (2012): The Cabin in the Woods was co-written by Joss Whedon and Drew Goddard in about three days.
The Cabin in the Woods was filmed in 2009 but sat on a shelf for about three years before release.
The Core (2003): The Core is often named by scientists as one of the least realistic science movies ever made.
The Disaster Artist (2017): The Disaster Artist is about the making of The Room, often called the best bad movie ever made.
James Franco directed The Disaster Artist while playing Tommy Wiseau, and stayed in character between takes.
The Drop (2014): The Drop was James Gandolfini's last movie. It's based on a short story by Dennis Lehane, who also wrote the script.
The Dukes of Hazzard (2005): The Dukes of Hazzard is based on the 1979 TV show. Lots of real Dodge Chargers were used, and many were wrecked doing jumps.
The Endless (2018): Directors Justin Benson and Aaron Moorhead also star in The Endless, playing brothers who share their own first names.
The Fog of War: Eleven Lessons from the: The Fog of War won the Oscar for Best Documentary. Errol Morris filmed it using his Interrotron, which lets people look straight into the camera.
The Foreigner (2017): The Foreigner is based on Stephen Leather's 1992 novel The Chinaman. Jackie Chan did his own stunts in his 60s.
The Greatest Game Ever Played (2005): The Greatest Game Ever Played was directed by actor Bill Paxton.
The Grey (2011): The Grey was filmed in freezing weather in British Columbia, and the actors' breath and shivering were real.
The Grinch (2018): Benedict Cumberbatch voices the Grinch with an American accent.
The Hot Chick (2002): Rachel McAdams appears in The Hot Chick two years before Mean Girls.
The Hunger Games: Mockingjay - Part 1 (2: The Hanging Tree song from Mockingjay - Part 1, sung by Jennifer Lawrence, became a real hit song.
The Hustle (2019): The Hustle is a remake of Dirty Rotten Scoundrels, which was itself a remake of the 1964 movie Bedtime Story.
Bar Rescue (2011): Jon Taffer, the host of Bar Rescue, says he came up with the idea behind NFL Sunday Ticket.
Barry (2018): Henry Winkler won his first ever Emmy for playing acting teacher Gene Cousineau in Barry.
BEEF (2023): BEEF was inspired by a real road rage incident that happened to creator Lee Sung Jin.
Bill Nye: The Science Guy (1993): Bill Nye was a mechanical engineer at Boeing before becoming the Science Guy.
Black Mirror (2011): Black Mirror is named after the dark, shiny screen of a phone or TV when it's turned off.
Cobra Kai (2018): Cobra Kai started on YouTube's paid service before moving to Netflix, where it became a huge hit.
Ralph Macchio and William Zabka play the same characters they played in The Karate Kid 34 years earlier.
Cosmos (2014): Neil deGrasse Tyson's Cosmos continues Carl Sagan's 1980 series, and Sagan's widow Ann Druyan co-wrote it.
Dark (2017): Dark was the first German-language series Netflix made.
Dark's young and old versions of each character were cast to look alike, sometimes matching eye colour with contact lenses.
Derry Girls (2018): Derry Girls is based on creator Lisa McGee's own teenage years in Derry, Northern Ireland, in the 1990s.
Dinosaurs (1991): Dinosaurs was made by Jim Henson's company, with actors inside large animatronic dinosaur suits.
Fleabag (2016): Fleabag started as a one-woman stage show by Phoebe Waller-Bridge at the Edinburgh Fringe festival.
Forged in Fire (2015): Doug Marcaida's line 'It will keel' from Forged in Fire became a famous internet meme.
Foundation (2021) (2021): Foundation is based on Isaac Asimov's books, long called impossible to film.
Fringe (2008): Hidden glyphs shown before ad breaks in Fringe spell out secret words when decoded.
Halo (2022): Halo's TV show is set in its own timeline, separate from the games' story.
The Adventures of Jimmy Neutron: Boy Gen: Jimmy Neutron: Boy Genius was nominated for the first ever Oscar for Best Animated Feature.
The Handmaid's Tale (2017): The Handmaid's Tale is based on Margaret Atwood's 1985 novel, and Atwood has a cameo in the first episode.
The Handmaid's Tale was the first streaming show to win the Emmy for Best Drama Series.
Berserk (1997): Berserk is based on Kentaro Miura's manga, which ran for over 30 years.
BLUE LOCK (2022): Blue Lock's manga was so popular in Japan that the Japan Football Association used it to promote the national team.
Cyberpunk: Edgerunners (2022): After Edgerunners came out, so many people went back to Cyberpunk 2077 that its player count jumped.
DAN DA DAN (2024): DAN DA DAN is based on Yukinobu Tatsu's manga, who once worked as an assistant on Chainsaw Man.
Demon Slayer: Kimetsu no Yaiba (2019): The Demon Slayer movie Mugen Train became the highest-grossing movie ever in Japan.
Food Wars! (2015): The recipes in Food Wars! were created by a real chef, Yuki Morisaki.
Fullmetal Alchemist: Brotherhood (2009): Brotherhood follows Hiromu Arakawa's manga all the way, while the 2003 Fullmetal Alchemist anime made up its own ending.
Hunter x Hunter (2011) (2011): Hunter x Hunter (2011) was made by studio Madhouse. Its creator, Yoshihiro Togashi, is married to Sailor Moon creator Naoko Takeuchi.
Back in Action (2025): Back in Action brought Cameron Diaz back to acting after about ten years away from movies.
Dracula Untold (2014): Dracula Untold tells the story of Vlad the Impaler, the real 15th-century prince who inspired Bram Stoker's Dracula.
Friends with Benefits (2011): Friends with Benefits came out the same year as No Strings Attached, a movie with almost the same idea.
Here Comes the Boom (2012): Kevin James trained for months in real mixed martial arts for Here Comes the Boom, and real UFC fighters appear in it.
Hostage (2005): Hostage is based on Robert Crais's novel, and Bruce Willis's real daughter Rumer plays his daughter.
I Now Pronounce You Chuck & Larry (2007): I Now Pronounce You Chuck & Larry was co-written by Alexander Payne, who later made Sideways and The Holdovers.
Idiocracy (2006): The fake sports drink Brawndo from Idiocracy was later sold as a real drink.
Inkheart (2008): Inkheart is based on German author Cornelia Funke's novel. She has said she had Brendan Fraser in mind when she wrote the hero.
Instant Family (2018): Instant Family is based on director Sean Anders's own experience adopting three siblings from foster care.
Invincible (2006): Invincible tells the true story of Vince Papale, a 30-year-old bartender who made the Philadelphia Eagles from an open tryout.
Jack and Jill (2011): Adam Sandler plays both twins in Jack and Jill, and Al Pacino plays a funny version of himself.
Jiro Dreams of Sushi (2011): Jiro Ono's tiny 10-seat sushi restaurant in a Tokyo subway station once had three Michelin stars.
Jobs (2013): Ashton Kutcher studied Steve Jobs so closely for Jobs that he copied his walk, and even tried his fruit-only diet.
Kedi (2017): Kedi follows street cats in Istanbul, filmed with cameras low to the ground at cat height.
Kill Bill: The Whole Bloody Affair (2011: The Whole Bloody Affair puts Kill Bill Volumes 1 and 2 together as one long movie, the way Quentin Tarantino first imagined it.
Kingpin (1996): Bill Murray did his own bowling in Kingpin, including some real strikes.
Let's Be Cops (2014): Jake Johnson and Damon Wayans Jr. were co-stars on the sitcom New Girl when they made Let's Be Cops.
Letters to Juliet (2010): Letters to Juliet is inspired by the real Club di Giulietta in Verona, whose volunteers answer letters written to Shakespeare's Juliet.
Lights Out (2016): Lights Out grew from director David F. Sandberg's short film, which went viral online in 2013.
Lightyear (2022): Lightyear is presented as the movie Andy watched that made him a Buzz Lightyear fan in Toy Story.
Little Nicky (2000): Little Nicky has a surprise cameo from rock star Ozzy Osbourne.
Love & Other Drugs (2010): Love & Other Drugs reunited Jake Gyllenhaal and Anne Hathaway, who had played husband and wife in Brokeback Mountain.
Man on Wire (2008): Man on Wire tells how Philippe Petit walked a tightrope between the Twin Towers in 1974. It won the Oscar for Best Documentary.
Men in Black: International (2019): Chris Hemsworth and Tessa Thompson had already played Thor and Valkyrie together before Men in Black: International.
Mother! (2017): Mother! was filmed in one house built on a soundstage in Montreal, and the camera almost never leaves Jennifer Lawrence.
My Neighbor Totoro (1988): Totoro is so loved that he became the logo of Studio Ghibli.
My Neighbor Totoro first came out in Japan as a double feature with Grave of the Fireflies.
My Octopus Teacher (2020): My Octopus Teacher won the Oscar for Best Documentary. Craig Foster visited the same octopus every day for about a year.
Nausicaä of the Valley of the Wind (1984: Nausicaä was so successful that it led to the founding of Studio Ghibli.
Hayao Miyazaki first made Nausicaä as a manga, and kept drawing it until 1994, ten years after the movie came out.
Norm Macdonald: Nothing Special (2022): Norm Macdonald recorded Nothing Special alone at home in 2020, the day before a medical procedure, in case it was his last chance.
Palm Springs (2020): Palm Springs sold at the Sundance Film Festival for a record-breaking amount, beating the old record by 69 cents.
Planes, Trains and Automobiles (1987): John Hughes wrote Planes, Trains and Automobiles in about three days.
The first cut of Planes, Trains and Automobiles was said to be about three to four hours long.
Pokémon Detective Pikachu (2019): Ryan Reynolds voices Pikachu and also did the facial motion capture for him.
Rebel Ridge (2024): Aaron Pierre took over the lead role in Rebel Ridge after filming had already started.
Red Dog (2011): Red Dog is based on a real dog who travelled around Western Australia in the 1970s. There's a statue of him in the town of Dampier.
Renfield (2023): Nicolas Cage plays Dracula in Renfield. He studied Bela Lugosi's classic performance to get it right.
Road House (2024): Road House (2024) is a remake of the 1989 Patrick Swayze movie, and real UFC fighter Conor McGregor makes his acting debut in it.
Robin Hood: Men in Tights (1993): Robin Hood: Men in Tights was Mel Brooks's spoof of Robin Hood: Prince of Thieves. Dave Chappelle has his first big movie role in it.
Rounders (1998): Rounders is often credited with helping start the big poker boom of the 2000s.
Santa Claus Is Comin' to Town (1970): Santa Claus Is Comin' to Town was made by Rankin/Bass with stop-motion puppets, and Fred Astaire narrates it as the mailman.
Scent of a Woman (1992): Al Pacino won his only Oscar for Scent of a Woman.
Al Pacino worked with blind teachers to learn how to play Lt. Col. Frank Slade without letting his eyes focus.
School Ties (1992): School Ties has an early cast of future stars, including Matt Damon, Ben Affleck and Chris O'Donnell.
Sergeant York (1941): Gary Cooper won the Oscar for Best Actor as Alvin York. The real York agreed to the movie only if Cooper played him.
Shark Tale (2004): In Shark Tale, the fish look a bit like the famous actors who voice them, like Will Smith and Robert De Niro.
She's the Man (2006): She's the Man is a modern take on Shakespeare's Twelfth Night. The school is named Illyria, like the play's setting.
Sinister (2012): Sinister was co-written by C. Robert Cargill, who got the idea from a nightmare after watching The Ring.
Small Soldiers (1998): Small Soldiers was the last movie for Phil Hartman, who voices one of the characters, and it was directed by Joe Dante of Gremlins.
Smart House (1999): Smart House was a Disney Channel Original Movie about a house run by a computer, years before smart speakers.
Spaceballs (1987): Spaceballs is Mel Brooks's spoof of Star Wars. George Lucas gave his blessing, as long as no toys were sold.
Mel Brooks plays two parts in Spaceballs: President Skroob and the wise Yogurt.
Starsky & Hutch (2004): Starsky & Hutch is based on the 1970s TV show, and the original stars, Paul Michael Glaser and David Soul, make a cameo.
Superbad (2007): Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg started writing Superbad when they were about 13 years old.
The two main characters in Superbad are named after the writers, Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg.
McLovin's famous fake ID in Superbad is a Hawaii driver's licence.
That's My Boy (2012): Andy Samberg plays Adam Sandler's grown-up son in That's My Boy, and Vanilla Ice plays himself.
The Boss (2016): Melissa McCarthy first created her character Michelle Darnell at the Groundlings comedy theater.
The League of Extraordinary Gentlemen (2: The League of Extraordinary Gentlemen is based on a comic by Alan Moore. It was Sean Connery's last live-action movie.
The Many Adventures of Winnie the Pooh (: The Many Adventures of Winnie the Pooh joins three Pooh short films into one movie. Walt Disney oversaw the first of them before he died in 1966.
The Ministry of Ungentlemanly Warfare (2: The Ministry of Ungentlemanly Warfare is based on a real secret British unit in World War II. Ian Fleming, who later wrote James Bond, worked near it.
The Running Man (2025): The Running Man (2025) is a new take on Stephen King's novel, which King first published under the name Richard Bachman.
The Social Network (2010): Aaron Sorkin's script for The Social Network was so long and fast-talking that director David Fincher made the actors speak quickly to fit it.
Armie Hammer played both Winklevoss twins in The Social Network, with another actor's body and Hammer's face added by computer.
The opening bar scene of The Social Network was filmed 99 times.
The Vast of Night (2019): The Vast of Night was made on a tiny budget, with director Andrew Patterson paying for much of it himself.
Thir13en Ghosts (2001): Thir13en Ghosts is a remake of William Castle's 1960 movie 13 Ghosts, which came with special glasses to see the ghosts.
Tommy Boy (1995): Chris Farley's Fat guy in a little coat bit in Tommy Boy was partly made up on the spot.
Turbo Kid (2015): Turbo Kid began as a short film entered in a contest for the horror anthology The ABCs of Death 2, then grew into a full movie.
Unbreakable (2000): Unbreakable became the first part of a trilogy with Split and Glass.
Undercover Brother (2002): Undercover Brother started as an online cartoon series.
Upgrade (2018): Upgrade was written and directed by Leigh Whannell, the co-creator of Saw. Logan Marshall-Green did his own robotic fight moves.
Waiting... (2005): Waiting... was written and directed by Rob McKittrick, based on his own years working in restaurants.
We Bought a Zoo (2011): We Bought a Zoo is based on the true story of Benjamin Mee, who bought a run-down zoo in England. The movie moves it to California.
Wet Hot American Summer (2001): Wet Hot American Summer was filmed in 28 days, and many of its unknown cast became big stars, including Bradley Cooper and Paul Rudd.
What Lies Beneath (2000): Robert Zemeckis made What Lies Beneath during a break in filming Cast Away, while Tom Hanks lost weight.
What Women Want (2000): Mel Gibson did real research for What Women Want, including trying on pantyhose and makeup.
White Chicks (2004): Shawn and Marlon Wayans spent hours each day in makeup to become the Wilson sisters.
Wild Hogs (2007): Wild Hogs has a cameo from Peter Fonda, the star of the biker classic Easy Rider.
Bo Burnham: What. (2013): Bo Burnham put his special What. on YouTube for free the same day it came out on Netflix.
Bo Burnham: Words, Words, Words (2010): Words, Words, Words was Bo Burnham's first full comedy special, made when he was just 19.
Jeff Dunham: Spark of Insanity (2007): Jeff Dunham's puppets, like Walter and Peanut, are all built by Dunham himself.
Loki (2021): The TVA offices in Loki were designed with a 1960s-70s retro look, using old-style computers and paper files.
Ozark (2017): Ozark is set at the Lake of the Ozarks in Missouri, but most of it was filmed in Georgia.
Peacemaker (2022): James Gunn wrote all eight episodes of Peacemaker's first season while in lockdown in 2020.
Peacemaker's dance-filled opening credits were choreographed by Charissa Barton, and the cast learned it for real.
Peaky Blinders (2013): The real Peaky Blinders were a Birmingham street gang said to sew razor blades into their caps, though historians doubt that part.
Planet Earth (2006): Planet Earth took about five years to make and was among the first nature series filmed in high definition.
Planet Earth's film crews used a helicopter camera called the Heligimbal, steady enough to film wolves and caribou from far away.
Pokémon (1997): Ash's Pikachu is voiced by Ikue Ōtani in every language, which is why it sounds the same everywhere.
Pikachu was picked as the star of the Pokémon anime because it was popular with girls as well as boys, and its yellow stood out.
Russian Doll (2019): Harry Nilsson's song Gotta Get Up plays over and over in Russian Doll. Getting the rights to it was hard and expensive.
Scooby-Doo, Where Are You! (1969): Scooby-Doo's name came from the end of Frank Sinatra's song Strangers in the Night, which goes doo-be-doo-be-doo.
Casey Kasem, the famous radio DJ, voiced Shaggy for over 40 years.
Silo (2023): Silo is based on Hugh Howey's Wool books, which he first sold himself as cheap e-books.
The giant spiral staircase in Silo was a real set, built several floors high.
Slow Horses (2022): Mick Jagger wrote and sings Slow Horses's theme song, Strange Game.
Succession (2018): Jeremy Strong stayed deep in character as Kendall Roy for much of Succession.
That '70s Show (1998): Mila Kunis lied about her age to get the part of Jackie in That '70s Show. She was 14, not 18.
The Orville (2017): Seth MacFarlane created The Orville as a love letter to Star Trek, and many Star Trek veterans directed episodes.
The Rookie (2018): The Rookie is loosely based on the true story of William Norcross, who joined the LAPD at age 45.
The Smurfs (1981): In the original French, Smurfs are called Les Schtroumpfs.
The Terminal List (2022): The Terminal List is based on Jack Carr's novel. Carr is a former Navy SEAL and has a cameo in the show.
Tokyo Vice (2022): Tokyo Vice is based on the memoir of Jake Adelstein, an American who became a crime reporter for a Japanese newspaper.
Trailer Park Boys (2001): Trailer Park Boys is filmed like a documentary in Nova Scotia, Canada, and started as a low-budget movie in 1999.
Mr Inbetween (2018): Scott Ryan wrote every episode of Mr Inbetween and stars as Ray. It began as his low-budget 2005 movie The Magician.
The Imagineering Story (2019): The Imagineering Story was made by Leslie Iwerks, granddaughter of Ub Iwerks, who helped create Mickey Mouse.
JoJo's Bizarre Adventure (2012) (2012): The JoJo's Bizarre Adventure manga started in 1987 and is still running.
Many JoJo powers are named after real bands and songs, like Killer Queen and Crazy Diamond.
One-Punch Man (2015): One-Punch Man started as a free webcomic by ONE, drawn very roughly. Artist Yusuke Murata later redrew it as a polished manga.
Tokyo Revengers (2021): Tokyo Revengers is based on Ken Wakui's manga. Wakui was once a member of a youth gang himself.
Yu-Gi-Oh! Duel Monsters (2000): Yu-Gi-Oh! began as a manga by Kazuki Takahashi, and the card game in the story became a real card game.
The Yu-Gi-Oh! trading card game holds a Guinness World Record as one of the best-selling card games.
Rascal Does Not Dream of Bunny Girl Senp: Rascal Does Not Dream of Bunny Girl Senpai is set in Fujisawa, Kanagawa, and fans visit its real locations.
Maoyu: Archenemy & Hero (2013): Maoyu began as a story posted on the Japanese message board 2channel.
GATE (2015): GATE was written by Takumi Yanai, a former member of Japan's Self-Defense Forces.
Gachiakuta (2025): Gachiakuta's graffiti art is designed by Hideyoshi Andou, a real graffiti artist who works on the manga.
MASHLE: MAGIC AND MUSCLES (2023): MASHLE's second season opening song, Bling-Bang-Bang-Born by Creepy Nuts, became a huge viral hit.
Call of the Night (2022): Call of the Night is by Kotoyama, the creator of Dagashi Kashi, and is named after a Creepy Nuts song.
Fate/Grand Order - Absolute Demonic Fron: Babylonia is based on the mobile game Fate/Grand Order and features King Gilgamesh, from the oldest written story in the world.
Love, Chunibyo & Other Delusions! (2012): Chūnibyō is a Japanese word for teens who act like they have secret powers, like a second-year middle schooler.
ReLIFE (2016): ReLIFE started as a webcomic on the Comico app, and all 13 episodes were released online at once.
A Fish Called Wanda (1988): John Cleese's character is named Archie Leach, which was Cary Grant's real name before he became a star.
Amadeus (1984): Tom Hulce practised the piano for hours every day so his hands would look right playing Mozart's music.
Bullet Train (2022): The stunt team said Brad Pitt did around 95% of his own stunts in Bullet Train.
Harvey (1950): James Stewart had already played Elwood P. Dowd, the man with the invisible rabbit friend, on Broadway before the movie.
Haunted Mansion (2023): Haunted Mansion is packed with nods to the Disneyland ride, like the stretching room and Madame Leota in her crystal ball.
Hereditary (2018): The tiny model rooms Annie builds in Hereditary were real miniatures made by a team of artists.
The Curious Case of Benjamin Button (200: For the early scenes, Brad Pitt's face was put by computer onto smaller actors, so the tiny old Benjamin is still him.
Titanic (1997): The hands drawing Rose's portrait in Titanic belong to James Cameron, not Leonardo DiCaprio.
Kate Winslet sent James Cameron a single rose with a card signed From Your Rose while she was trying to win the part.
The crew nicknamed James Cameron Mij, which is Jim spelled backwards, for his tough side on set.
James Horner wrote My Heart Will Go On in secret, because Cameron didn't want a pop song in the movie.
The Titanic set faced the wrong way, so departure scenes were filmed mirrored, with signs and costumes reversed, then flipped back.
Prometheus (2012): Ridley Scott didn't tell actress Kate Dickie what a creature scene would involve, so her scream is real.
Some sounds in Prometheus were made with Pop Rocks candy and a sound designer's pet parrot.
Composer Marc Streitenfeld wrote some of the music backwards, had the orchestra play it, then flipped the recording.
Ridley Scott wanted round glass helmets with no blind spots, inspired by a story about Steve Jobs and Gorilla Glass.
American Psycho (2000): Christian Bale made up Patrick Bateman's moonwalk on the spot.
Christian Bale was paid only about $50,000 to play Patrick Bateman.
Bale based Bateman's manner partly on Tom Cruise's very intense friendliness in a David Letterman interview.
Christian Bale stayed in character for the whole shoot, even speaking with an American accent off camera.
Bring It On (2000): The Bring It On cast went to a four-week cheerleading camp so the movie wouldn't need stunt doubles.
Kirsten Dunst first turned down the role of Torrance.
Crazy Rich Asians (2018): The fake stuffed tiger in the Young family home was held up by customs officers who thought it was a real one.
Director Jon M. Chu is mentioned in the original novel, because author Kevin Kwan was friends with Chu's cousin.
Constance Wu wrote to the director about why she had to play Rachel, and filming was pushed back four months so she could.
The Warriors (1979): For the big gang meeting at the start of The Warriors, real gang members were used as extras, with off-duty police in the crowd.
The Warriors' big Bronx gang meeting was actually filmed in Riverside Park in Manhattan.
Akira (1988): Akira was drawn by hand using over 160,000 drawings, far more than most animated movies of its time.
Akira used 327 colours, and about 50 of them were mixed just for this movie.
Apollo 13 (1995): The floating scenes in Apollo 13 were filmed for real inside NASA's zero-gravity plane, about 25 seconds at a time.
The real Jim Lovell has a cameo in Apollo 13 as the captain of the recovery ship.
Coraline (2009): Coraline's tiny knitted sweater was hand-made by an artist using needles about as thin as a human hair.
Coraline was the first stop-motion feature filmed in 3D.
Bridesmaids (2011): Rebel Wilson improvised for an hour in her Bridesmaids audition and won a part.
The Iron Giant (1999): Vin Diesel voices the Iron Giant.
The Iron Giant himself was animated on a computer, then made to blend in with the hand-drawn characters around him.
Reservoir Dogs (1992): Michael Madsen wanted to play Mr. Pink, but Quentin Tarantino insisted he play Mr. Blonde.
The robbers' colour code names were borrowed from the 1974 movie The Taking of Pelham One Two Three.
Quentin Tarantino plays Mr. Brown in Reservoir Dogs.
The Green Mile (1999): Shaquille O'Neal has said he turned down the role of John Coffey.
Tom Hanks was going to play the old Paul too, but the makeup tests didn't look convincing.
The Black Cauldron (1985): The Black Cauldron was the first Disney animated movie rated PG.
American Gangster (2007): Denzel Washington has 64 costume changes in American Gangster.
The Patriot (2000): The Patriot's costume team studied real Revolutionary War uniforms at the Smithsonian before filming.
Cowboys & Aliens (2011): Director Jon Favreau's face is on a wanted poster in Cowboys & Aliens, under the name Todd Kravitz.
Slumdog Millionaire (2008): Some of Slumdog Millionaire's child actors were real kids from Mumbai's slums.
Baby Driver (2017): Many scenes in Baby Driver were planned and cut to match the exact beats of the songs Baby is listening to.
Baby Driver's car chases were done with real cars and stunt drivers, with very few computer effects.
Elemental (2023): Elemental is based on director Peter Sohn's own family, Korean immigrants who ran a grocery store in New York.
Dogma (1999): Emma Thompson was first set to play God in Dogma. Alanis Morissette took the part.
World War Z (2013): World War Z's whole last act was rewritten and reshot after the first version didn't work.
Apocalypto (2006): The actors in Apocalypto speak the Yucatec Maya language the whole way through.
Apocalypto used animatronics and puppets for its animal scenes so no real animals were hurt.
Tower Heist (2011): Gabourey Sidibe and Eddie Murphy's safe-cracking scene is the only improvised scene in Tower Heist.
Demolition Man (1993): In Demolition Man's future, Taco Bell is the only restaurant left. Some countries' versions changed it to Pizza Hut.
Wesley Snipes turned down Demolition Man several times, so the producers flew to another movie's set to win him over.
Black Widow (2021): Jeremy Renner has a secret voice-only cameo in Black Widow.
Solaris (2002): Steven Soderbergh also filmed and edited Solaris himself, under made-up names in the credits.
Beauty and the Beast (2017): Dan Stevens wore tall stilts as the Beast, and had to learn to waltz on them for the ballroom scene.
10,000 BC (2008): One frame of the mammoths took about 16 hours to make, so the team removed half their computer fur to save time.
10 Cloverfield Lane (2016): 10 Cloverfield Lane was made in secret under the fake name Valencia. Its Cloverfield link was a surprise until shortly before release.
10 Cloverfield Lane was filmed in story order, almost all on one set.
A History of Violence (2005): Harrison Ford turned down the lead role in A History of Violence.
1917 (2019): 1917 was filmed and edited to look like one long continuous shot.
The crew dug over a mile of real trenches for 1917.
101 Dalmatians (1961): Disney used a new photocopying trick on 101 Dalmatians, which saved animators from inking every single spot by hand.
A Charlie Brown Christmas (1965): The Peanuts kids were voiced by real children. Some were too young to read, so they learned their lines bit by bit.
TV executives thought A Charlie Brown Christmas would flop. It became one of the most-watched holiday specials ever.
A Few Good Men (1992): Aaron Sorkin first wrote A Few Good Men as a play, partly on cocktail napkins while working as a Broadway bartender.
Air Bud (1997): Buddy, the golden retriever in Air Bud, really could shoot basketball hoops.
Almost Famous (2000): Almost Famous is based on Cameron Crowe's own teenage job writing about rock bands for Rolling Stone.
Armageddon (1998): Ben Affleck asked Michael Bay why NASA didn't just train astronauts to drill. Bay told him to be quiet.
Babe (1995): Babe was played by 48 different piglets, because real pigs grow too fast to film for long.
Bohemian Rhapsody (2018): Rami Malek wore false teeth to play Freddie Mercury.
Brave (2012): Merida was Pixar's first main character who is a girl.
Braveheart (1995): Many of the soldiers in Braveheart's battle scenes were members of the Irish army reserve.
Caddyshack (1980): Bill Murray made up the famous Cinderella story scene in Caddyshack on the spot.
Cast Away (2000): Cast Away stopped filming for a year so Tom Hanks could lose weight and grow his beard.
Wilson the volleyball got so famous that the real Wilson company sold a version with his face.
Catch Me If You Can (2002): The real Frank Abagnale has a cameo in Catch Me If You Can as a French police officer.
Charlie and the Chocolate Factory (2005): Tim Burton used real trained squirrels to crack nuts in the nut room scene, not computer ones.
Chef (2014): Roy Choi, the chef who started the famous Kogi taco trucks, taught Jon Favreau to cook for Chef.
Children of Men (2006): The car ambush in Children of Men was filmed in one take, using a special camera rig built into the car.
Clue (1985): Clue came out in cinemas with three different endings. Each cinema showed just one of them.
Contact (1997): Contact used real news clips of President Bill Clinton, and the White House complained about it.
Dazed and Confused (1993): Matthew McConaughey's line Alright, alright, alright was made up on the spot. It was his first scene in a movie.
Django Unchained (2012): Leonardo DiCaprio cut his hand on a glass during a scene and kept acting. That take is in the movie.
Dunkirk (2017): Christopher Nolan used real ships and real World War II planes in Dunkirk.
E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial (1982): Reese's Pieces sales jumped after E.T. The makers of M&M's had turned down the chance to be in the movie.
Part of E.T.'s voice came from a woman named Pat Welsh, who had a raspy voice.
Edward Scissorhands (1990): Johnny Depp speaks only about 169 words in all of Edward Scissorhands.
Elf (2003): Some of Elf's New York street scenes were filmed with hidden cameras, so many passers-by reactions are real.
Will Ferrell said eating so much sugar as Buddy gave him headaches.
Face/Off (1997): Nicolas Cage and John Travolta studied each other's habits so they could swap characters halfway through Face/Off.
Fantasia (1940): Fantasia was one of the first movies shown with stereo sound. Disney called its system Fantasound.
Fargo (1996): Fargo says it is a true story at the start, but it isn't. The Coen brothers made it up.
Ferris Bueller's Day Off (1986): The red Ferrari in Ferris Bueller's Day Off was mostly replicas. The real one was too valuable to crash.
Fight Club (1999): David Fincher has said there is a Starbucks cup in almost every scene of Fight Club.
Forgetting Sarah Marshall (2008): The Dracula puppet musical in Forgetting Sarah Marshall was a real project Jason Segel had been working on for years.
Forrest Gump (1994): Gary Sinise wore blue stockings on his legs so they could be removed by computer for Lieutenant Dan.
Tom Hanks's younger brother Jim was his double for many of Forrest's running scenes.
Full Metal Jacket (1987): R. Lee Ermey, who plays the drill sergeant, was a real Marine drill instructor and came up with many of his own insults.
Godzilla Minus One (2023): Godzilla Minus One won the Oscar for visual effects with a budget of under $15 million and a small effects team.
Good Will Hunting (1997): Robin Williams made up the story about his wife's funny habits. Matt Damon's laughter is real, and you can see the camera shake.
GoodFellas (1990): Joe Pesci's famous Funny how? scene in GoodFellas is based on something that really happened to Pesci.
Grease (1978): Olivia Newton-John had to be sewn into her tight black trousers for the last scene of Grease.
Groundhog Day (1993): Bill Murray was bitten twice by the groundhog while filming Groundhog Day.
Hook (1991): Glenn Close has a hidden cameo in Hook, playing a bearded male pirate.
Hot Fuzz (2007): Cate Blanchett has a secret cameo in Hot Fuzz, with her face hidden behind a mask.
How the Grinch Stole Christmas (2000): Jim Carrey found the Grinch makeup so hard to wear that he got tips from a man who trained spies to handle torture.
Inception (2010): Inception's spinning hallway fight was filmed in a real hallway set that turned all the way around.
Interstellar (2014): Christopher Nolan had about 500 acres of real corn planted for Interstellar, and later sold it.
Interstellar's black hole visuals were so accurate that the science team wrote real research papers about them.
Joker (2019): The Bronx stairs Joker dances down became a tourist spot after the movie came out.
La La Land (2016): La La Land's opening number was filmed on a real closed-off freeway ramp in Los Angeles.
Les Misérables (2012): The actors in Les Misérables sang live on set instead of miming to recordings.
Life of Brian (1979): Beatle George Harrison mortgaged his house to pay for Life of Brian after the first backers pulled out.
Marley & Me (2008): Marley was played by 22 different dogs.
Minority Report (2002): Steven Spielberg had real scientists dream up future technology for Minority Report, and its glove screens inspired real research.
Monty Python and the Holy Grail (1975): The knights in Holy Grail bang coconuts together instead of riding horses, partly because they couldn't afford horses.
Mrs. Doubtfire (1993): Robin Williams improvised so much in Mrs. Doubtfire that some scenes were filmed in family-friendly and grown-up versions.
My Cousin Vinny (1992): Real lawyers often praise My Cousin Vinny as one of the most accurate courtroom movies ever made.
Napoleon Dynamite (2004): Jon Heder was paid about $1,000 to play Napoleon Dynamite.
Office Space (1999): Office Space grew out of Mike Judge's short cartoons about Milton, the mumbling worker with the red stapler.
Oppenheimer (2023): Oppenheimer's Trinity test explosion was made without computer effects.
Pan's Labyrinth (2006): Doug Jones played both the Faun and the Pale Man, and learned his Spanish lines by sound.
Parasite (2019): The rich family's house in Parasite isn't a real home. It was a set built for the movie.
Pulp Fiction (1994): The glow inside the famous briefcase in Pulp Fiction came from a hidden orange light bulb.
Ratatouille (2007): The fancy version of ratatouille Remy makes was designed by famous real chef Thomas Keller.
Saving Private Ryan (1998): The main cast went through army boot camp, but Matt Damon was left out on purpose so the others would resent him.
Se7en (1995): Brad Pitt really broke his arm during a chase in Se7en, so his character's arm is in a cast afterwards.
Shaun of the Dead (2004): Many zombie extras in Shaun of the Dead were fans of Simon Pegg and Edgar Wright's TV show Spaced.
The Shawshank Redemption (1994): Morgan Freeman spent a whole day throwing a baseball for one Shawshank scene, without complaining.
The Shining (1980): Jack Nicholson made up the line Here's Johnny! in The Shining.
The Silence of the Lambs (1991): Anthony Hopkins is on screen for only about 16 minutes in The Silence of the Lambs, and still won Best Actor.
Snakes on a Plane (2006): Snakes on a Plane added scenes and its famous line after fans online made the title a giant joke.
Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs (1937): People in Hollywood called Snow White Disney's Folly, because they were sure a full-length cartoon would flop.
Team America: World Police (2004): Team America was made with real string puppets. Trey Parker called it one of the hardest things he ever made.
The Big Lebowski (1998): Jeff Bridges wore a lot of his own clothes to play the Dude.
The Blair Witch Project (1999): The Blair Witch actors filmed it themselves with little script. The directors left them notes and surprises in the woods.
The Breakfast Club (1985): The Breakfast Club was filmed mostly in story order, in a real school building.
The Dark Crystal (1982): The Dark Crystal has no human actors on screen. Every character is a puppet.
The Fifth Element (1997): Luc Besson started writing The Fifth Element as a teenager.
The Fugitive (1993): Tommy Lee Jones made up his famous I don't care! line in The Fugitive.
The Goonies (1985): The Goonies kids hadn't seen the pirate ship before filming, so their amazed faces in that scene are real.
The Nightmare Before Christmas (1993): Jack Skellington had about 400 swappable heads to show his different expressions.
The Polar Express (2004): Tom Hanks plays six different characters in The Polar Express.
The Princess Bride (1987): Billy Crystal made Rob Reiner laugh so hard that Reiner had to leave the set.
André the Giant had a bad back, so in scenes where Fezzik carries people, they were often held up by ramps or wires.
The School of Rock (2003): The kids in School of Rock really played their own instruments.
The Sixth Sense (1999): The colour red shows up in The Sixth Sense whenever the spirit world is close by.
The Terminal (2004): The airport in The Terminal was a full-size set built inside an aircraft hangar.
The Truman Show (1998): Truman's perfect hometown was filmed in a real Florida town called Seaside.
The Wizard of Oz (1939): Dorothy's ruby slippers are silver in the original book. They were made red to show off the new colour film.
The first actor cast as the Tin Man got sick from the aluminium powder makeup and had to be replaced.
The Wolf of Wall Street (2013): Matthew McConaughey's chest-thumping hum in The Wolf of Wall Street was his real warm-up routine.
Up (2009): Pixar animated 20,622 balloons for the moment Carl's house lifts off.
WALL·E (2008): WALL-E's voice was made by Ben Burtt, the sound designer who also created R2-D2's beeps.
When Harry Met Sally… (1989): The woman who says I'll have what she's having is director Rob Reiner's mother.
Who Framed Roger Rabbit (1988): Mickey Mouse and Bugs Bunny share a scene in Roger Rabbit, and got exactly equal screen time.
Willy Wonka & the Chocolate Factory (197: Gene Wilder took the part only if he could come out limping with a cane and then do a somersault.
Breaking Bad (2008): Vince Gilligan pitched Breaking Bad as turning Mr. Chips into Scarface.
Bryan Cranston got the role partly because Vince Gilligan remembered him from an X-Files episode Gilligan wrote.
Better Call Saul (2015): Saul Goodman's name is a joke: say it fast and it sounds like S'all good, man.
The Office (2005): The Scranton shots in The Office's opening were filmed by John Krasinski himself before he got the part.
Rainn Wilson first auditioned for Michael Scott.
Parks and Recreation (2009): Chris Pratt's Andy was only meant to be in the first season, but the writers loved him and kept him.
Brooklyn Nine-Nine (2013): When Fox cancelled Brooklyn Nine-Nine, fans protested online and NBC picked it up about a day later.
Community (2009): Donald Glover was a writer on 30 Rock when he was cast in Community.
Futurama (1999): Futurama hides messages in alien alphabets that fans worked out how to read.
The Simpsons (1989): Matt Groening named Homer, Marge, Lisa and Maggie after his own family. Bart is an anagram of brat.
South Park (1997): The first South Park episode was made with real construction-paper cutouts.
SpongeBob SquarePants (1999): SpongeBob's creator, Stephen Hillenburg, was a marine biology teacher before he became a cartoonist.
Avatar: The Last Airbender (2005): Each kind of bending is based on a real martial art. Waterbending comes from Tai Chi, and Toph's earthbending from Southern Praying Mantis.
Game of Thrones (2011): The Dothraki language in Game of Thrones was made up by linguist David J. Peterson, with thousands of real words.
The direwolf pups in the first season were played by real Northern Inuit dogs.
Stranger Things (2016): The Duffer Brothers' pitch for Stranger Things was turned down by around 15 to 20 networks.
Stranger Things was first called Montauk.
Lost (2004): Lost's crash site used a real airliner body, cut into pieces and shipped to Hawaii.
Doctor Who (2005): The TARDIS's famous whooshing sound was first made by scraping a key along a piano's strings.
Firefly (2002): Firefly was cancelled after one season, but fans made so much noise that it got a movie, Serenity.
The Mandalorian (2019): Grogu was a real puppet on set, worked by a team of puppeteers.
Much of The Mandalorian was filmed inside the Volume, a giant ring of LED screens showing the worlds around the actors.
Arcane (2021): Arcane took about six years to make.
Chernobyl (2019): Chernobyl was partly filmed at a shut-down nuclear power plant in Lithuania that is very like the real one.
The Wire (2002): Felicia Pearson, who plays Snoop in The Wire, had never acted before. Actor Michael K. Williams spotted her in a Baltimore club.
Severance (2022): Lumon's headquarters in Severance is the real old Bell Labs building in New Jersey, once a famous science research center.
Ted Lasso (2020): Ted Lasso started as a set of TV adverts for Premier League football in America in 2013.
Schitt's Creek (2015): Schitt's Creek was created by a real father and son, Eugene and Dan Levy, who also play father and son.
The Last of Us (2023): Several voice actors from The Last of Us games appear in the show, including Troy Baker and Ashley Johnson.
Wednesday (2022): Jenna Ortega came up with Wednesday's famous school dance moves herself.
The Witcher (2019): Henry Cavill is a huge fan of The Witcher games, and lobbied hard to play Geralt.
Malcolm in the Middle (2000): The family's last name in Malcolm in the Middle is never clearly said.
King of the Hill (1997): Mike Judge voices both Hank Hill and Boomhauer.
It's Always Sunny in Philadelphia (2005): The first version of It's Always Sunny was shot on a home video camera for a tiny amount of money.
Rick and Morty (2013): Rick and Morty began as a rude cartoon parody of Back to the Future's Doc and Marty.
Scrubs (2001): Scrubs was filmed in a real former hospital in North Hollywood.
Arrested Development (2003): Ron Howard is the narrator of Arrested Development, and later shows up as himself.
Bluey (2018): Bluey's dad, Bandit, is voiced by Dave McCormack, the singer of Australian rock band Custard.
Ed, Edd n Eddy (1999): Ed, Edd n Eddy was one of the last big cartoons drawn and painted by hand on cels.
Death Note (2006): L sits crouched in chairs because he says his thinking drops by 40% if he sits normally.
Attack on Titan (2013): Hajime Isayama's Attack on Titan was turned down by Weekly Shōnen Jump before another magazine took it.
One Piece (1999): The One Piece manga has sold over 500 million copies, more than any other comic by one author.
Dragon Ball (1986): Dragon Ball is loosely based on the old Chinese story Journey to the West. Goku is named after its Monkey King, Sun Wukong.
Sailor Moon (1992): Sailor Moon's creator, Naoko Takeuchi, is married to Yoshihiro Togashi, the creator of Hunter x Hunter.
Bleach (2004): Tite Kubo nearly gave up after an early manga was cancelled, until Akira Toriyama sent him an encouraging letter.
House (2004): Hugh Laurie is English, and filmed his House audition in a hotel bathroom in Namibia. The producers thought he was American.
The Big Bang Theory (2007): A real physicist checked The Big Bang Theory's whiteboards so the equations were correct.
Torchwood (2006): Torchwood is an anagram of Doctor Who. It started as a code name for secret Doctor Who tapes.
Babylon 5 (1994): Babylon 5 was one of the first TV shows to make its spaceships entirely with computer graphics.
Planet Earth II (2016): The famous chase of a baby iguana by racer snakes in Planet Earth II was filmed in the Galápagos Islands.
The Expanse (2015): After The Expanse was cancelled, fans flew a banner over Amazon's studios, and Amazon picked it up.
Star Wars: The Clone Wars (2008): Ahsoka Tano was created for The Clone Wars before getting her own show.
Kim's Convenience (2016): Kim's Convenience started as a stage play by Ins Choi, who also plays Jung's friend Kimchee.
Letterkenny (2016): Letterkenny began as short YouTube videos called Letterkenny Problems.
Jury Duty (2023): Everyone in Jury Duty was an actor except juror Ronald Gladden, who thought it was a real trial.
The Queen's Gambit (2020): Chess champion Garry Kasparov helped plan the chess games in The Queen's Gambit.
WandaVision (2021): WandaVision's first episode was filmed in front of a live studio audience, like an old sitcom.
The Umbrella Academy (2019): The Umbrella Academy comic was created by Gerard Way, the singer of My Chemical Romance.
